scenario.name: Elastic Security Labs — Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor
scenario.shortSubtitle: Elastic Security Labs · GUP.exe libcurl.dll Side-Loading, MurmurHash API & CHRYSALIS Implant
scenario.overview: Picture an international border crossing checkpoint with glass passport inspection booths, zig-zag queue stanchions, an X-ray luggage conveyor belt, and a striped crossing barrier. Approaching the international border crossing, a traveler steps up to the glass passport booth carrying a travel booklet with a subtly altered entry stamp. In this real-world scenario, the intruder steps up to the luggage x-ray belt & barrier blending in with everyday guests, then smuggles copied records out past the luggage x-ray belt & barrier in tiny disguised batches. A secondary customs officer cross-checks the border passport registry and catches a stamp serial number that was never issued by that embassy. In this scenario (T1574.002, Elastic Security Labs, Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: dropping a Legitimate Signed Binary, then aPI Hashing, then establishing Persistence. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Dropping a Legitimate Signed Binary, then API Hashing, then Establishing Persistence, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 7 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: WINGUP (GUP.EXE) DLL SIDE-LOADING OF LIBCURL.DLL
stages.subtitle: Signed GUP.exe loads trojanized libcurl.dll from C:\ProgramData\NotepadPlus
stages.description: Approaching the international border crossing, a traveler steps up to the glass passport booth carrying a travel booklet with a subtly altered entry stamp. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder steps up to the luggage x-ray belt & barrier blending in with everyday guests while everyday visitors and the border customs officer go about their routine. Across campaigns analyzed by Elastic Security Labs and Cisco Talos, the attacker stages a 3-file triad inside a writable folder like C:\ProgramData\Comms\: (1) a genuine, digitally signed executable (such as Microsoft’s MsMpEng.exe or Notepad++ WinGUp GUP.exe, authentic signed binaries whose valid digital certificates prevent antivirus from blocking the .exe launch), (2) a malicious companion DLL named mpclient.dll or libcurl.dll placed in that exact same folder (exploiting Windows’ default DLL search order, which checks the application’s current directory before C:\Windows\System32), and (3) an encrypted data file named chrysalis.dat or conf.bin (containing the actual backdoor in scrambled form so static file scanners see only random bytes). When the signed host binary starts from C:\ProgramData\Comms\, the Windows loader (ntdll!LdrLoadDll) resolves its Import Address Table (IAT), sees an import for mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll, finds the attacker’s unsigned DLL sitting in the local directory first, and maps it directly into the trusted process. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 exchange from Lotus Blossom C2 Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SIDELOAD LIBCURL request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 FNV-1A / MURMURHASH API RESOLUTION & CHRYSALIS DECRYPTION). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SIDELOAD LIBCURL / ⇠#1 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ① (#1 Lotus Blossom C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM).

stages.title: FNV-1A / MURMURHASH API RESOLUTION & CHRYSALIS DECRYPTION
stages.subtitle: Dynamic PEB walking and in-memory decryption of gup.dat payload
stages.description: While the customs scanner checks only the outer cover of the passport, the forged interior page clears the glass booth and the striped crossing barrier swings upward. Here in Step 2 inside the border control, the intruder uses borrowed access inside the border control to slip closer to the passport glass inspection booth without disturbing the diplomatic sealed pouch lane. Once the signed binary loads the trojanized DLL and calls its exported startup function (keeping the malicious DLL tiny and using custom 32-bit API hashing instead of plaintext function names like VirtualAlloc so static analysts see no suspicious imports), the DLL opens the companion file chrysalis.dat / conf.bin from disk, decrypts its bytes in RAM using a custom RC4/XOR key, and copies the unpacked Chrysalis / Sagerunex shellcode into an executable memory buffer (meaning the actual APT backdoor code only ever exists in volatile memory, never unencrypted on the hard drive). Splitting the infection chain across three files (a clean signed .exe, a minimal loader .dll using API hashing, and an encrypted .dat/.bin blob) defeats traditional signature scanners: the .exe is 100% legitimate, the .dll contains only a simple file-read and XOR/RC4 loop, and the .dat file has no PE header ("MZ") on disk. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CHRYSALIS UNPACK / ⇠#2 ALERT 164 KB RWX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM).

stages.title: CHRYSALIS HTTPS C2 BEACON & INTERACTIVE RECON
stages.subtitle: Encrypted C2 channel from GUP.exe and internal network enumeration
stages.description: Rolling luggage smoothly off the X-ray conveyor into the secure arrival hall, the traveler crosses the border wearing an official-looking entry clearance. In this final step inside the border control, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the luggage x-ray belt & barrier in tiny disguised batches until the customs passport registry catches the mismatch. Running inside the trusted host binary, the decrypted Chrysalis/Sagerunex implant registers a persistent Windows service or Registry Run key (pointing to the legitimate signed .exe so startup monitors see a signed binary), and calls Windows WinInet APIs (InternetOpenW and HttpSendRequestW, chosen instead of raw sockets because WinInet automatically reads the logged-in employee’s corporate proxy settings and cached NTLM/Kerberos credentials, allowing the C2 beacon to pass right through strict enterprise web proxies). In many enterprise networks, direct outbound TCP/443 connections are blocked unless traffic authenticates through a corporate HTTP proxy. Using WinInet with INTERNET_OPEN_TYPE_PRECONFIG lets the malware piggyback on Windows’ built-in proxy configuration and user credentials automatically. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp) to libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM, libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM responds with ACK TLS 1.2 (confirming that the HTTPS C2 BEACON request succeeded on libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM and completing the final execution objective of Elastic Security Labs, Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HTTPS C2 BEACON / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.2) from Node ③ (#3 GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp)) to Node ④ (#4 libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM).

detectionRule.title: WinGUp (GUP.exe) DLL Side-Loading Unsigned libcurl.dll
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Lotus Blossom WinGUp libcurl.dll Side-Loading
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\GUP.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\libcurl.dll'
    Signed: 'false'
  condition: selection
level: high
detectionRule.mitigation: Enforce Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) / AppLocker rules blocking unsigned DLL loads from C:\ProgramData\ and user-writable folders.

detectionRule.title: GUP.exe Executing from Non-Standard Path Making Network Connections
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Suspicious Outbound Network Connection by Relocated GUP.exe
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\GUP.exe'
    Initiated: 'true'
  filter_legit:
    Image|startswith:
      - 'C:\Program Files\Notepad++\'
      - 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Notepad++\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: high
detectionRule.mitigation: Restrict GUP.exe execution to official Program Files paths and block outbound connections from binaries running out of C:\ProgramData\.
